answer: The submission is clear and honest, but it reads as a well-meaning concept paper rather than an investable plan. Priority improvements, roughly in order of impact: (1) Quantify the problem and market. Replace 'several thousand neurologists' and 'a meaningful business' with a bottom-up model: number of target clinics x patients per clinic x realistic enrollment rate x price. Cite sources for prevalence, visit frequency and tremor prevalence (not all Parkinson's patients have significant tremor, so the addressable population is smaller than one million). Show the math behind the $50K ARR projection, which currently implies only about $250/patient/year and looks modest for the effort. (2) Reframe candor as a plan. The team repeatedly admits gaps (no validation, unconfirmed reimbursement codes, no regulatory expertise, no entity, no website) but mostly leaves them as open items. For each, state the specific next step, owner, timeline and cost, e.g., validation study design (sample size, comparator such as MDS-UPDRS tremor items, success threshold like correlation >0.8), and what the prize money buys at each stage. (3) Address regulatory and compliance risk directly. Software that scores a symptom for clinical decision-making may qualify as a Software as a Medical Device, and storing patient video triggers HIPAA, BAAs, and consent and security obligations. The plan should state the intended-use claim (monitoring vs. diagnostic), the likely FDA pathway, and how video storage costs and privacy will be handled (e.g., retaining only extracted metrics versus raw video). (4) Resolve the reimbursement uncertainty. The business model hinges on clinics being able to bill (e.g., RPM CPT codes), yet this is unconfirmed. Note that RPM codes generally have device and data-day requirements that a video-based web app may not meet; investigate this early, since it determines whether clinics will pay. Offer a fallback value proposition if billing is not possible (time savings, better visits, retention). (5) Strengthen evidence of traction. The paid pilot is the strongest asset but is described vaguely. Give the number of patients, duration, fee, adherence rate (do patients actually record daily?), clinician feedback, and any early quality signals. Adherence and video quality (lighting, camera angle, tremor from handheld device) are key technical risks to discuss. (6) Sharpen the competitive analysis. Name specific competitors (e.g., wearable-based tools such as Apple Watch Parkinson's features, Kinesia, PD telemonitoring platforms), compare on accuracy, cost, effort and clinical validation in a table, and explain defensibility: video-based scoring is replicable, so articulate the moat (proprietary dataset, clinical validation, clinic workflow integration, EHR integration). (7) Fix team and structure gaps. The lack of a physician or regulatory/reimbursement expertise is a core weakness; name the advisor and define their role, and recruit a regulatory/health-policy advisor. Settle the founder equity split and entity formation before seeking funding, since investors will see this as a basic execution risk. (8) Tighten the financials. Add a simple 12-24 month budget, burn, unit economics (gross margin after cloud/video storage, CAC, clinic onboarding effort), and clear milestones the funding unlocks. (9) Improve the document itself. Add an explicit ask amount, remove vague language ('alot', 'effects' for 'affects', 'several thousand'), add a one-paragraph vision/long-term opportunity (pharma trial endpoints, essential tremor), include a product screenshot or workflow diagram, and cut repetition so the executive summary is a true summary rather than a full-length narrative.
